subject: Semtools in combination with Lavaan fit to get Mc Donald's omega vs bootstrapped result

messages.author: b430763ad49e6cd0
messages.subject: Semtools in combination with Lavaan fit to get Mc Donald's omega vs bootstrapped result
parts:
Dear all,

I have fit a longitudinal CFA and have been reading up on some reliability measures. I found in many papers that Cronbach's alpha usually makes too strong or unrealistic assumptions and that McDonald's omega (1999) is probably better to use instead. Less assumptions and more realistic ones. In this paper: http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/wol1/doi/10.1111/bjop.12046/full the authors provide an easy to use bootstrap tutorial for computing omega's point estimate + confidence interval. 

This result however differs quite heavily from the result I get from semTools::reliability(fit), where the point estimate is about 0.08 lower. 
Outputs:



The package used for the bootstrap is 'MBESS' and the data that is used in the function are the same four indicators that are used in the CFA I fit using Lavaan. 

I was wondering the reason for this?

Kind regards,

Amonet

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Semtools in combination with Lavaan fit to get Mc Donald's omega vs bootstrapped result
parts: I was wondering the reason for this?

It would surprise me if these differed, since Sunthud wrote the source code for both semTools::reliability() and MBESS::ci.reliability().  Note that MBESS::ci.reliability() uses factor loadings from a 1-factor model, whereas semTools::reliability() uses factor loadings from your fitted model, which looks like a 4-factor model.  If you are not using equivalent models, the parameter estimates will differ, and so therefore will omega.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 9e44085005cccdfd
messages.subject: Re: Semtools in combination with Lavaan fit to get Mc Donald's omega vs bootstrapped result
parts:
Dear Terrence,

I have two questions related to this topic: I am using semTools::reliability() to estimate categorical omega ("oemga3" in semTools) for my 4-factor model with categorical items. However, on one factor these results differ markedly compared to those I get when I estimate omega for each factor separately.

Full 4-factor model results (omega3):
PE: 0.7544268
RE: 0.8329719
EV: 0.7664426
SH: 0.8359911

Separate analyses model results (omega3):
PE: 0.8812945 (!!!)
RE: 0.8207932
EV: 0.7528306
SH: 0.8369976

As one can see the main difference pertains to factor PE (8 items). This is interesting as here I had to include three pairs of correlated residuals to account for method effects. However, I would not suspect this to be the reason for differences as both models (4-factor & PE as 1-factor) contain these correlated residuals (plus two more in the  4-factor model). So why does omega3 differ so markedly for this one factor (PE), but barely for the others?


My second question is more general: is there some sort of "built-in" option in  semTools to get confidence intervals of reliability estimates? I know that  MBESS::ci.reliability() can be used for this purpose. However, this is not an option for me as it would ignore the correlated residuals in my model.
As a workaround I found the following solution (see https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45121311/bootstrap-to-get-confidence-intervals-using-r):

library(semTools)
library(boot) # Bootstrap Functions

### example ###
data <- HolzingerSwineford1939

model <- 'visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

# function to reliability stats
reliability <- function(formula, data, indices) {
  data = data
  d <- data[indices,] # allows boot to select sample
  fit <- cfa(model, data=d)
  semTools::reliability(fit)
}

# bootstrapping with 1000 replications
boot.out <- boot(data=data, statistic=reliability, R=1000, formula=model, parallel = 'snow')

# Retrieve the Omega and confidence intervals
CI_omega <- boot.ci(boot.out, conf = 0.95, type="bca", index = 4)
omega <- CI_omega$t0
omega.ci <- CI_omega$bca[,c(4,5)]

Interestingly, using this I get the follwing results for my 4-factor model where now PE does not differ so  markedly anymore!
        estimate       lower CI   upper CI
PE:            0.855    0.816    0.887
RE:            0.809    0.758    0.857
EV:            0.767    0.666    0.832
SH:            0.837    0.779    0.878

Would be great to have your view about this. Thanks in advance & kind regards,
Jan

I read that e.g. cronbach's alpha would require unidimensional settings.

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Semtools in combination with Lavaan fit to get Mc Donald's omega vs bootstrapped result
parts:
Jan

To understand the difference between the single factor and the 4 factor model, can you show the factor loadings for the PE factor for both? The omega3 is calculated based on these, so if the 4 factor model loadinsg differ from the single factor model, that would be the reason of the differences.

Other things that could be affecting this, missing data,

For another thread I wrote a little code to get bootstap reliability measures from the semTools function, using the bootstrap function in lavaan instead of boot


library(lavaan)
library(semTools)


## The famous Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3

textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, std.lv=T,
           data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE)

rels_fun <- function(obj){
  temp0 <- reliability(obj)
  temp <- c(temp0[1,], temp0[4,], temp0[5,])
  names(temp) <- c(paste0(c("alpha_"),
                          colnames(temp0)),
                   paste0(c("omega3_"),
                          colnames(temp0)),
                   paste0(c("ave_"),
                          colnames(temp0)))
  return(temp)  
}


bts <- bootstrapLavaan(fit, R=1000,
                       FUN=rels_fun,
                       type="ordinary")
bts
#### 95% quantile CI, and median
t(apply(bts, 2, function(x) quantile(x, c(.025, .5, .975)) ))

parts:
Hernandez

The code I use for bootstrap uses the lavaan object to estimate the CI for alpha and Omega.
In my example since I am treating the items as continuous with estimator="ml" (default) it will use the covariance matrices to estimate them.
If you specify in the cfa function that some/all items are categorical and estimator="wlsmv" (default with categorical items), them the estimated alpha dna omega will be calculated with the polychorical correlation matrix. The semTools function is smart enough to use the correct matrix depending of the type of item specified in cfa()

Would only need to change this

fit <- cfa(HS.model, std.lv=T,
           data = HolzingerSwineford1939,
ordered=T, estimator="wlsmv")

parts:
Jan

As soon as you have difference in residual covariances, Omega3 is more sensitive sensitive to these differences.

See in this example, that Omega3 is the one that presents bigger differences, specially when there is a resicual covariance present in one of the models, even in this case that the residual correlation is not large r = -.19



library(lavaan)

The code I use for bootstrap uses the lavaan object to estimate the CI for alpha and Omega.
In my example since I am treating the items as continuous with estimator="ml" (default) it will use the covariance matrices to estimate them.
If you specify in the cfa function that some/all items are categorical and estimator="wlsmv" (default with categorical items), them the estimated alpha dna omega will be calculated with the polychorical correlation matrix. The semTools function is smart enough to use the correct matrix depending of the type of item specified in cfa()

           data = HolzingerSwineford1939,

For another thread I wrote a little code to get bootstap reliability measures from the semTools function, using the bootstrap function in lavaan instead of boot


library(lavaan)
library(semTools)


## The famous Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, std.lv=T,
           data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE)

rels_fun <- function(obj){
  temp0 <- reliability(obj)
  temp <- c(temp0[1,], temp0[4,], temp0[5,])
  names(temp) <- c(paste0(c("alpha_"),
                          colnames(temp0)),
                   paste0(c("omega3_"),
                          colnames(temp0)),
                   paste0(c("ave_"),
                          colnames(temp0)))
  return(temp)  
}


bts <- bootstrapLavaan(fit, R=1000,
                       FUN=rels_fun,
                       type="ordinary")
bts
#### 95% quantile CI, and median
t(apply(bts, 2, function(x) quantile(x, c(.025, .5, .975)) ))

My second question is more general: is there some sort of "built-in" option in  semTools to get confidence intervals of reliability estimates? I know that  MBESS::ci.reliability() can be used for this purpose. However, this is not an option for me as it would ignore the correlated residuals in my model.
As a workaround I found the following solution (see https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45121311/bootstrap-to-get-confidence-intervals-using-r):

library(semTools)
library(boot) # Bootstrap Functions

### example ###
data <- HolzingerSwineford1939

model <- 'visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

# function to reliability stats
reliability <- function(formula, data, indices) {
  data = data
  d <- data[indices,] # allows boot to select sample
  fit <- cfa(model, data=d)
  semTools::reliability(fit)
}

# bootstrapping with 1000 replications
boot.out <- boot(data=data, statistic=reliability, R=1000, formula=model, parallel = 'snow')

# Retrieve the Omega and confidence intervals
CI_omega <- boot.ci(boot.out, conf = 0.95, type="bca", index = 4)
omega <- CI_omega$t0
omega.ci <- CI_omega$bca[,c(4,5)]

Am I correctly applying the Omega coefficient given this context? (i.e.: longitudinal factor model, with 1 factor measured at 4 time points). 
I read that e.g. cronbach's alpha would require unidimensional settings. 

Omega estimates the reliability of a composite, such as a scale sum or scale mean across items.  If you want to estimate omega for the scale separately at each occasion, I imagine your 4-factor model will provide valid estimates, to the degree that your model is specified correctly.
